Industry observers note that after building your Reachy Mini, you'll install the conversation app and start talking to it. Until now, you had to send your audio to a server. But not anymore. Today we'll walk you through running the whole stack locally.

Sources indicate that this stack is powered by speech-to-speech, our cascaded VAD → STT → LLM → TTS pipeline that exposes a Realtime API-compatible /v1/realtime WebSocket. Once you launch the backend, point the robot at it from the UI.

According to recent reports, cascades are the most flexible option in the open-source landscape today, and with the right pieces they're also the fastest. We'll recommend the components we like best, but the whole point of a cascade is that you can swap them. New models drop every week.

This blog walks you through running conversations with Reachy Mini fully locally. No cloud, no API keys, no data leaving your machine. Here's a video showing this live:.

According to recent reports, A cascaded voice pipeline has four stages: VAD, STT, LLM, and TTS. For three of them, we pick solid defaults so you can focus on the LLM:.

We are opinionated about these choices, feel free to swap them out for your own if you have a preference.

In a recent development, the LLM is the layer with the most impact on latency and overall performance of the system. We support two options: run a model locally (llama.cpp, MLX, Transformers, vLLM), or use a server with a Responses API (OpenAI, Gemini, HF Inference Endpoints, llama.cpp, vLLM, etc).

The main bottleneck in the system is LLM inference latency. To address that, we support external inference engines exposed through the Responses API protocol.

The speech-to-speech engine therefore supports a second mode where the LLM lives in a separate process as long as it speaks the Responses API protocol. You launch your model server in one terminal, you launch the voice loop in another terminal, and the two talk over HTTP.

It has been revealed that the --speculative-config line enables Multi-Token Prediction (MTP). It is optional, but it has a great impact on end-to-end latency. Leave it on whenever the model supports it.

Terminal 2: speech-to-speech client:.

Inside the Craft of the Snapple Rebrand 2026 by Deutsch Design

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deutsch Design restores Snapple's 90s racetrack logo in the Snapple rebrand 2026, rebuilt with custom letterforms and flavor-first packaging.
  • The change starts with the mark itself.
  • Recent findings suggest that the letterforms were drawn from zero, more geometric and less condensed than the 90s original, with the big curling S leading the wordmark and the strokes built to hold their weight at any scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deutsch Design restores Snapple's 90s racetrack logo in the Snapple rebrand 2026, rebuilt with custom letterforms and flavor-first packaging.

The change starts with the mark itself. The navy serif Snapple script sits tilted inside a white capsule, ringed in Racetrack Red on a field of Snapple Blue, and the whole thing reads at a glance, on a bottle or on a phone screen. The lowercase blue sans serif from the 2021 rebrand is gone, and with it the flat, generic feel that had crept in over a series of rebrands. What replaces it is warmer and louder: bolder color, higher contrast, and a shape that people who grew up with the brand recognize before they read a word.

Recent findings suggest that the letterforms were drawn from zero, more geometric and less condensed than the 90s original, with the big curling S leading the wordmark and the strokes built to hold their weight at any scale. A construction grid shows the mark measured out at 1X and 4X, and a second spread draws the letters as outlines with their bezier points exposed, annotated with notes on how the curves cue taste appeal. The supporting type is Cygnet CF by Connary Fagan, shown in 18 styles across 9 weights, set huge in magenta over raspberry photography.

On the bottle, each flavor gets its own world. Snapple Apple bursts across green with sliced apples and leaves, Raspberry Tea goes full magenta with whole raspberries around the bottle, and the ten-bottle lineup indicates the range working as one shelf, from Peach Tea to Orangeade. The fruit is shot big and close, so the taste feels immediate before a single word is read.

The palette is specced out in full: Snapple Blue at #10079E, Snapsolutely Blue at #004EE0, Racetrack Red at #E10800, and Zero Sugar White, each with hex, RGB, CMYK and PMS values. Real Tea and Real Juice badges sit on the labels, and the headline notes it plain: Sometimes you just want a drink that tastes good.

The rebrand was led by Deutsch Design in Los Angeles, with Adhemas Batista as chief design officer and Erica Park as group design director. See more from Deutsch Design on Behance.

Profiling in PyTorch (Part 1): A Beginner's Guide to torch.profiler

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you are trying to squeeze more tokens per second out of a Large Language Model (LLM), shave milliseconds off inference, or just understand why your training loop runs slower than the spec sheet promises, the path eventually runs through profiling.
  • In a recent development, the catch is that profiling has a steep on-ramp.
  • This is the opening post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What you cannot profile, you cannot optimize.

Whether you are trying to squeeze more tokens per second out of a Large Language Model (LLM), shave milliseconds off inference, or just understand why your training loop runs slower than the spec sheet promises, the path eventually runs through profiling.

In a recent development, the catch is that profiling has a steep on-ramp. The traces are dense walls of colored rectangles. The events carry intimidating names. Most tutorials assume you can already read them. So even when we know we should be profiling, opening a trace can feel like a chore best left for later (or for someone else). This post, and the series it kicks off, is our attempt to lower that on-ramp.

This is the opening post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.

In a recent development, we document the journey from a beginner's point of view. No prerequisites apart from basic PyTorch. Treat this as a leisurely read with some "Aha!" moments. The structure of the post is intentionally question-led: we open a trace, ask "wait, why is that happening?", and chase the answer until something clicks. By the end you should know:.

Before we begin, two definitions that will make everything below read better:.

You don't usually have to write GPU kernels yourself; when you use a PyTorch operation, it is automatically translated to one or more kernels that do the job on GPU.

With those two ideas in your back pocket, let's start asking questions.

Sources indicate that here is the entire script that we use for the post: 01_matmul_add.py. We recommend opening this script in a separate tab and walk through the code step by step. We use the NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to setup a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using the Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.(Note: The traces in this blog were generated using PyTorch 2.13. If you are using a different version, some trace details like CompiledFxGraph might differ or be absent.).

Recent findings suggest that as correctly quipped by Dr. Sara Hooker, just as we are primarily made up of water, Deep Neural Networks are primarily made up of matrix multiplies. As fundamental as they are, it would be a shame to start our profiling journey with anything else.

The matrix addition along with the matrix multiplication mimics how weights and biases interact in a neuron. This addition (pun intended) will help us understand how it paves the way for compilation later in the post.

To profile, we will be using the torch.profiler module. The steps involved are:.

The profiler exports two distinct artifacts:.

According to recent reports, let's see the two in action with our first execution. (Here is the entire 01_matmul_add.py script).

It is recommended to run this script on a machine with a GPU.

If you run the above script (on a GPU machine) you will find a folder traces/01_matmul_add with the two artifacts:.

In a recent development, the .txt file holds the profiler table. Upon opening the file, as shown in Figure 1, one would be greeted with a significant table with the first column consisting of the events that were triggered inside the scope of profile.

The other columns are related to the time the event takes on the CPU or GPU or any other device(s) specified in activities within torch.profiler.profile. Look at which events take the most amount of time, and try to intuitively understand if that event should in fact take that time. It is also vital to look at the column "# of Calls" which dictates how many times the event was triggered.

It has been revealed that while we are at it, let's also talk about "Self CPU/CUDA" vs "CPU/CUDA total". The "Self" columns measure time spent only inside the event itself, excluding its children. The "total" columns include the event and all of its children together. So if you look at the "CPU total" of matmul_add, it consists of the time it took on self plus the children events it triggered. This is an important nuance to note.

If you look at the last two lines out of the table you would notice that the profiler tells us that.

The CPU time is in ms while the GPU time is in us. To put things in perspective, the time spent on GPUs (the kernel ampere_bf16_s16816gemm...) is less than 1% of the time spent on the CPU (the matmul_add operation). The GPU stays idle most of the time, which is an immediate red flag. The reason this happens is that the GPU can compute a small matmul very quickly, so our code spends most of the time preparing the kernels, launching them on the GPU, sending the data to multiply and gathering the results. This concept is known as an overhead-bound algorithm.

The easiest way to move out of this regime is to use bigger matrix multiplications.

The last two lines in Figure 2 are:.

Sources indicate that both times are in ms, which means we have materialized more GPU time just by increasing the size of the matrix multiplications. If you look at Figure 2 you would also notice that the most CUDA time is now taken by the GPU kernel (ampere_bf16_s16816gemm_..) and not by the CPU operation that introduced it (matmul_add). This means that we were indeed able to move from overhead bound to compute bound.

We now move into visualising the dispatch chain, which lives inside the .json artifacts. You can upload them to Perfetto UI and see the traces, or you can use uvx trace-util -f traces -b /traces to generate the Perfetto links directly.

Sources indicate that in Figure 3, we see the profiler trace for the matrix multiplication and addition. Here the bar width indicates the duration of an event, the vertical nesting is the call hierarchy, the CPU lane denotes the events that happen on the CPU, while the GPU lane highlights the actual kernel executions. One might also notice the empty spaces which are the waiting or idle time.

The script was run with default configurations which are:.

In a recent development, with Perfetto we suggest using the keyboard for quicker access to the trace. One could use "W A S D" for navigating the trace.

Recent findings suggest that there are two lanes in Figure 4, one for the CPU activity and one for the GPU activity. In the CPU lane one would notice three profile steps (starting from ProfilerStep#2). This comes from the schedule.

Recent findings suggest that the wait skips noisy initializations (ProfilerStep#0), warmup runs through the profiler without recording (ProfilerStep#1), and active is what shows up in trace. One can find the schedule being used in the script here.

Let's put on our detective hats and investigate the trace and ask some questions.

According to recent reports, in Figure 5, we notice that ProfileStep#2 takes more time compared to the other steps, and upon looking closely you would see a similar pattern with the matmul_add annotation as well. The smoking gun is inside the annotation, not the annotation itself:.

That ~228 µs shown in Figure 6 is the "dead window" between entering record_function("matmul_add") and PyTorch actually dispatching aten::matmul. This can happen for multiple reasons, including workspace allocations, cuBLAS (NVIDIA’s proprietary, GPU-accelerated library for performing fundamental linear algebra operations) heuristics, or lazy module loading. We can either look away or run some more warmup steps before we profile (which is the standard).

Recent findings suggest that in terms of profiling, warmup is when you run the events a couple of times before actually profiling it. The pre-work done by the GPU (including the above pointers) are one time efforts which we do not want to profile. In our example, we have two warmup stages, one where we actually loop over the function before entering the profiler, and two inside the profiler which is achieved by the warmup argument. In this section, we have enabled the actual iterations along with the schedule.

Perfetto Trace for 64x64 with Warmup.

According to recent reports, in Figure 7 we see that each profile step takes a similar time, but this does not mean we were able to optimize the one time overheads. We warmed up the runs so that the overheads were not profiled. We think that closing this section abruptly without a hint to solving this would do injustice to the reader, so here is a link to read about further optimizing launch overheads.

In Figure 8, we see that the CPU and GPU lanes have an offset of around 2.5 ms: this is the delay after the CPU submits the CUDA kernels and the time they actually start executing. One might think the warmup stage combined with the schedule's wait and warmup should keep a GPU busy and would diminish the offset.

To uncover what is really happening, let's change our schedule a little:.

Figure 9 demonstrates us that there is an Activity Buffer Request in the GPU lane before any operation. Let's zoom in a little more.

Upon zooming into the GPU trace, we notice that the matmul and add kernels for ProfileStep#0 (the CPU trace of which is not visible in the Figure) happen one after the other, while the kernels for ProfileStep#1 have a window in between. The best explanation for this is that there was an overflow of buffers, and another buffer request (a request to allocate some memory on the GPU VRAM) was issued during the kernel execution.

The best way to rule out other possibilities is to profile for more iterations and see whether a similar window appears in other parts of the trace. To do that we run with active=20.

As shown in Figure 11, we see a similar trend in ProfileStep#1. This is aligned with our previous findings, and we can safely conclude that it was indeed another buffer request.

It has been revealed that in Figure 12, we see the nested CPU calls. This is an vital visualization, where one gets to understand what a chain of dispatch really looks like.

According to recent reports, we begin with ProfileStep# which encapsulates the profiling step. Due to us annotating the step, we see the matmul_add row. The matmul_add consists of two aten calls, one for matrix multiplication and one for matrix addition.

Industry observers note that the aten::matmul is the ATen-level dispatch that those user-facing PyTorch matmul calls land on. aten::mm is the 2D matrix-matrix multiply backend.

In a recent development, it is very interesting to note how PyTorch calls aten::bmm (batched matrix multiplication) if we add the batch axis to our matrices. Let's take a detour and see the aten::bmm in action.

According to recent reports, in Figure 13, upon adding the batch axis to the inputs, aten::matmul now encapsulates a bunch of other prerequisite CUDA runtime calls along with aten::bmm (instead of aten::mm). This also hints at the heuristics that cuBLAS needs to do in order to dispatch the right (most suitable) kernel for the program.

In the rest of the post, we will be working with simple 2D matrices, unless otherwise mentioned.

We notice that for aten::mm there are two CUDA Runtime calls, namely cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor (boxed in Figure 14) and cudaLaunchKernel, while for aten::add there is only the cudaLaunchKernel.

Recent findings suggest that cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor is a planning call and is purely CPU side. It asks: "given a kernel function, a chosen block size, and a chosen dynamic shared memory size, how many blocks of this kernel can simultaneously reside on one SM (Streaming Multiprocessor)?".

This begs the question, why do we need planning for matmul and not for add?

To understand this, we have to look at the kernel's resource footprint. If you click on the GPU kernels, you will be able to inspect the resource footprint for the respective kernel.

In Figure 15, we note that for matrix multiplication the registers per thread and shared memory are dynamic (based on the size of the matrix). cuBLAS ships hundreds of kernel variants, and each has a heuristic-driven launch path that needs runtime information about hardware capacity. The occupancy query is part of that heuristic. Conceptually, we can think of GPU-accelerated matmuls as working on independent tiles: how many tiles we use and how substantial each tile needs to be depends on the matrices and the hardware. Modern algorithms are way more complicated than that, but this is still a good reference framework.

According to recent reports, from Figure 16 we see that the footprint of addition claims 32 registers and zero shared memory. That fits trivially. There's nothing to query, because no hardware resource is going to limit occupancy. The kernel is, by design, resource-light.

According to recent reports, you can use this as a quick diagnostic when reading any trace. Scan the CPU lane for cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor. Each occurrence flags a "heavyweight, adaptively rolled out" kernel, usually a GEMM (GEneral Matrix Multiplication), conv, or similar. The kernels without a preceding occupancy query are the elementwise/reduction crowd that PyTorch debuts mechanically.

According to recent reports, cudaDeviceSynchronize blocks the CPU until all GPU work on this device finishes. The profiler emits this sync at the end of the active window to flush events. Without it, kernel timings would be missing.

Industry observers note that A 1.78 ms sync covering 26 µs of real GPU work tells you this run was 98% idle. That's the textbook overhead-bound symptom.

We already know from the profiler table analysis (above) that providing bigger matrices to our algorithm moves it out from the overhead-bound region to being compute-bound.

Let's run the command and dive deeper into the traces.

Recent findings suggest that in Figure 17, we notice that the matmul kernel for ProfileStep#3 takes longer on the GPU than the other steps. This is particularly interesting to note, because the other kernels rolled out were the exact same, which means there were no cuBLAS heuristics involved. There are no scheduling gaps, the CPU launches are normal, and it is not a profiler artifact.

This trace in Figure 17 makes a useful point that's easy to miss in idealized examples: kernel runtimes are not constants, even on the same hardware environment running identical code on identical data.

Let's make this more concrete by modifying the script a little. We run the iteration 20 times, capturing each of the steps.

Figure 18 reveals a similar finding. While each kernel was the exact same, they time differently. The different compute times can be blamed on a bunch of reasons:.

Industry observers note that A reader who only saw the average would conclude that a matmul took ~1 ms (mean of 5 = 1084 µs); a reader who looked at the trace would see that the matmul takes ~580 µs except when the GPU throws a fit. Those are very different mental models, and only one of them is correct.

According to recent reports, working with torch.compile has always amazed us. One writes normal eager PyTorch code, but PyTorch tries to capture tensor-heavy regions, turn them into graphs, optimize them, and run generated code. The default backend is usually TorchInductor, and the broad pipeline is:.

In this section, we talk about compilation and look at the profiler traces.

The args.compile flag triggers the following code:.

In Figure 19, we see the fresh CPU rows named Torch-Compiled Region: 0/0 which points us to the compiled functions being used.

Looking at Figure 20 we ask the question, did we actually fuse the multiplication and addition operations together into one?

This is operator fusion at the graph level. Inductor took our torch.add(torch.matmul(x, w), b) and rewrote it into a single aten::addmm(b, x, w) call. The key thing to note here is that it did not produce a newly introduced fused CUDA kernel. The actual GPU work is still ampere_bf16_s16816gemm_bf16_128x256_ldg8_f2f_stages_64x3_nn, the same cuBLAS kernel eager mode used. So the "fusion" here is at the dispatcher level, not at the kernel level.

It has been revealed that pyTorch provides the torch.addmm function that does what we did in two steps, that is multiply and add. We encourage the reader to look at the traces of this function and comment your observations in the comments below!

Recent findings suggest that while we know in theory what happens when we compile our functions it is equally notable to see it in action. Let's look at the CPU-side hierarchy which reflects torch.compile's runtime architecture.

Industry observers note that torchDynamo Cache Lookup is where Dynamo checks that the current call still matches what was compiled with the same input shapes, dtypes, devices, and tensor metadata. If anything mismatched, Dynamo would recompile. This cost is paid every call, even after compilation.

Recent findings suggest that torch-Compiled Region is the wrapper that "enters" the compiled version. AOTDispatcher Runtime Wrapper Prologue is AOT Autograd's runtime wrapper. Even though we don't need gradients here, AOTDispatcher is always in the stack handling tensor metadata, view tracking, and would set up the backward pass if requires_grad were true.

Sources indicate that ## Call CompiledFxGraph is where the actual generated code runs. The string after "CompiledFxGraph" is the content hash of the FX graph. It's the same across all three active steps, confirming cache hits.

You can find the generated code on disk under /tmp/torchinductor_/fxgraph keyed by this hash, useful when you want to read the Triton/C++ that Inductor actually produced.

Looking at the traces in Figure 21, we were really happy to notice only one cudaLaunchKernel per step. This observation was directly contradicting what we were seeing in the GPU trace. There were still two kernels being introduced per step, namely the Memcpy DtoD (Device -> Device) and the GEMM. Going back to the CPU trace, we noticed that we had completely missed the cudaMemcpyAsync dispatch.

Recent findings suggest that addmm computes out = α·A·B + β·C, and cuBLAS's GEMM-with-bias-add epilogue writes into a destination buffer that needs to already contain the bias. An epilogues can be thought of all the operations that happen after a GEMM. In the world of deep-learning we constantly come up with GEMM-Epilogues like activations, bias addition, normalization and many more. This is why there are cuBLAS GEMM-with- kernel variants.

In a recent development, if you use different modes for torch.compile you would notice different kernel variants being released. You can try it for yourself and add a comment below about your observations!

So Inductor-generated code does:.

The result is mathematically still the same. The bias add isn't free, as we pay a memcpy upfront plus a slightly more expensive GEMM epilogue.

The fusion one might have hoped for, where x·w + b (here out = α·A·B + β·C) collapses into a single kernel with no extra memory traffic, isn't what happened. Inductor preserved the two memory-touching operations, it just relabeled the bias copy as a memcpy and the addition as a GEMM epilogue.

It has been revealed that A truly fused implementation would skip the memcpy. That's what FlashAttention-style hand-written kernels do, and what Inductor can do via Triton codegen, but for a 4096×4096 bf16 matmul, Inductor evidently decided "use cuBLAS, do the bias via epilogue setup" was the best path.

This is the easiest thing to miss when comparing an eager and a compiled run:.

torch.compile is roughly 2× more expensive on the CPU per step. That's because every call walks the full Dynamo > AOTAutograd > Inductor stack, on top of the same aten::addmm dispatch we have anyway. The compile pipeline is built for ML models with dozens of ops where the per-call overhead amortizes (for a single op it's a tax).

torch.compile has a mode argument. It is for the reader to take home as an assignment to read the documentation and come up with a mode that could take the CPU overhead down. 🤗.

It has been revealed that A quick reference for the patterns we walked through. The idea is: if you see this in a trace, this is what it usually means.

We started with a tiny matmul + add and used it as an excuse to learn how to read a PyTorch profiler. Along the way we picked up a few mental models that travel well to bigger workloads. This was the first stop in the Profiling PyTorch series. In the posts that follow, we will gradually leave this two-op toy behind and walk up the ladder of complexity, looking at larger building blocks and, eventually, real models.

Thanks to Noe Flandre, Suvaditya Mukherjee, and Vidit Ostwal for their reviews on the early draft of the post!

The blog post was polished using an LLM. This in no way means that we have let an agent run in the background and let it generate the blog. Some of us in the team are non-english speakers and think LLMs (which are mostly trained in the English Language) can rectify silly grammar mistakes or rephrase sentences that sound less intimidating and cleaner. Hope this helps with the idea of "why should I read, if this was LLM generated". 🤗.

You are right with your observation about cudaMemcpyAsync vanishing and only one kernel launch ..._ldg8_relu_f2f_stages_64x3_nn. It turns out that the new kernels is a relu family kernel, which does the EPILOGUE properly where it falls under the contract of using a bias and broadcasting it across rows. Previously the bias was 2D and did not fall under the correct EPILOGUE contract, and hence there was an extra cudaMemcpyAsync.

Industry News: Beyond LLMs: Why Scalable Enterprise AI Adoption Depends on Agent Logic

📅 01 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that guides have aided humanity throughout history.
  • In a recent development, numerous studies have cited the overwhelming failure of AI pilots, while others have also highlighted the need for AI to operate at the core of enterprise workflows to enable scalable adoption.
  • Possess a plethora of APIs, databases and servicesC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that guides have aided humanity throughout history. Prehistoric civilizations understood that the sun and the moon could be used to navigate vast distances on land and the high seas. Over time, various journeys facilitated the production of maps for better planning and faster travel time to repeat destinations. Centuries later, the introduction of the compass enabled seagoers to achieve greater accuracy in seeking unexplored destinations. And today, GPS navigation apps guide our every journey. In today’s world of agentic AI, AI agents, admittedly, have the potential to enable scalable AI adoption, transforming industries as we know them. However, an intelligent guide, agentic logic, is needed to realize this potential by fueling high agent quality, cost-effectiveness, and consequent end-user trust.

Enterprise Workflows & Use Cases.

In a recent development, numerous studies have cited the overwhelming failure of AI pilots, while others have also highlighted the need for AI to operate at the core of enterprise workflows to enable scalable adoption. [1] [2] To better understand this phenomenon and the associated assertion, some analysis of enterprise workflows is required. These workflows are:.

A. Dynamic and long-runningB. Possess a plethora of APIs, databases and servicesC. Oftentimes are constrained by business policies and/or regulations.

For an agent to function effectively, given these above characteristics, naturally demands an expanded model context, which state-of-the-art frontier LLMs certainly possess, but at what tradeoff? Increased hallucinations, token consumption? Further, can LLMs be equipped with an intelligent guide, GPS, to enable agentic AI execution at the core of the workflow, driving more desirable outcomes? We tested these hypotheses by designing and building agents, equipped with pertinent agent logic, for IBM offerings fully considering the above characteristics. These offerings pertain to some of the most challenging tasks confronting subject matter experts who own various stages of the enterprise software delivery lifecycle for mission critical workloads including:.

It has been revealed that before examining each of these domains in detail, let us define what characterizes agent logic. Agent logic is software primitives, such as knowledge graphs, algorithms, program analysis libraries, which operate at the agentic layer (within an agent harness) and can intentionally steer the LLM in the direction of the enterprise workflow, reducing the context space. In so doing, have strong tendency to drive more performant outcomes in a more cost-effective manner. Let us now examine how agent logic is able to achieve such outcomes in each of the above four domains.

IBM watsonx Code assistant for Z (WCA4Z), used to accelerate mainframe application development and modernization with AI and automation, is equipped with an App Insights agent for application understanding - one of the primary focus areas of enterprise clients running mission critical workloads on IBM mainframe. This agent leverages deep static analysis across the application and stores a pre-indexed representation in a database schema that spans hundreds of interrelated tables with complex semantics, allowing the agent to retrieve precise, structured already available information; thereby improving answer accuracy, reducing token usage, and minimizing back-and-forth interactions with the language model (Mistral Medium 250B in this instance). This approach when applied to multiple mission-critical legacy systems (up to 1M lines of code and 1K programs) maintains marginally superior app understanding performance with ~30× lower token consumption than a baseline frontier LLM-only approach.

Aster is an IBM proprietary program analysis and data pre- and post-processing-based library utilized for agent-based generation of unit, integration, API and change-based tests; which from analysis of multiple developer communities achieves higher developer ratings compared with various open-sourced tools or developer-written tests. Based on the latter and superior line, branch and method coverage benchmarks compared with similar open-sourced tools (integration tests) and zero-shot LLMs and coding agents (unit tests), all tested on open-sourced applications, we have been running Aster in pre-production mode on 75+ java IBM CIO applications (up to 560+ classes and 67K+ lines of code) with Devstral 24B model. Steady-state results to date yield +20% - 45% improvement in line, branch and method coverage coupled with superior performance on a subset of these apps compared with state-of-the-art coding agent with orders of magnitude lower token consumption (up to 15×). The rationale for these results is that the program analysis output (used to prompt and “focus” the LLM) coupled with sub-agents for augmenting coverage and remediating runtime and compilation errors enable a more performant outcome with significant cost reduction.

It has been revealed that while LLM context for app-related use cases as described in 1 and 2 are “restricted” to the app source code, for runtime management of apps on deployed infra, the underlying IT full stack comes into play. Here we define a knowledge graph (KG) encompassing entities (microservices, database/middleware services, MELT etc.) coupled with embedded (“tribal”) knowledge from domain experts. With such a graph and bounding the LLM to local bound reasoning for non-deterministic outcomes, an observability-driven approach is used to achieve reduced context space spanning the IT stack and underlying app source code (if relevant) for incident root cause analysis (and other use cases). With this approach, leveraging the equivalent Instana data model, we have seen the proprietary Instana “I3” (intelligent incident investigation [8]) agent achieve up to 4.0× improvement over ReAct agent with GPT-5.1 as measured using ITBench [9]. With Gemini 3 Flash the ReAct agent performance improves to within 17% lower than the I3 agent while consuming 1.6× more tokens, We have extended this approach to source code with agents for code analysis (leveraging program dependency graphs) and bug remediation (leveraging inference scaling), also tested on ITBench, illustrating superior performance for the source code analysis and bug remediation agents (Gemini 2.5 Flash) over state-of-the-art coding agent both for finding the culpable microservice (3.0×) and bug repair (1.6×) while consuming respectively 3.7× and 5.9× less tokens. This multi-agent system was announced at IBM Think as part of the newly unveiled IBM Concert Platform for shift-left IT Operations and is also being piloted internally with IBM CIO. [10].

Enterprises face increasingly complex and fragmented compliance requirements, forcing teams to spend considerable time manually creating controls, assessments and remediation aims. No centralized knowledge exists and fixes are written manually, which introduces a risk of errors and security gaps. Because compliance work is complex and multi-step, it requires coordinated policy-driven automation across specialized agents rather than manual effort or simple AI prompts. Our multi-agent system automates compliance by algorithmically decomposing complex tasks into coordinated steps, using adaptive planning, dynamic decomposition and workflow sequencing with continuous feedback to iteratively identify fixes and expand assessments. It is 1.3 – 2.0× more performant than prior agents (Claude 4 Sonnet) using fixed planning strategies, as also measured using ITBench. This approach transforms compliance into a continuously guided self-correcting process and dramatically improves outcomes, especially in complex scenarios, boosting success rates from single digits to as high as +80% (Claude 4 Sonnet). This multi-agent system and 16K+ digitized controls mappings were unveiled as part of IBM Sovereign Core at IBM Think, integrated with monitoring, drift detection, providing automated evidence generation, ensuring audit evidence stays securely within customer control. [12].

The above examples illustrate the impact of agent logic in reducing LLM context and guiding the LLM to traverse the core of the workflow in a highly performant and cost-effective manner. Additionally, we have employed similar approaches to two case studies, one with a configurable generalist agent and runtime (CUGA) in the healthcare domain and another for the condition-based maintenance for physical assets with IBM Global Real Estate.

Industry observers note that case Study 1: Configurable Generalist Agent (CUGA) Healthcare benchmark - algorithmic policy enforcement. [13].

Sources indicate that the following health insurance customer care example is a compact illustration of why agentic systems outperform LLM-only conversational models in regulated environments. CUGA’s (configurable generalist agent) policy system implements policy-as-code for agent governance, which is enforced at runtime independent of model prompts and without fine-tuning. Our experiments show that the agent’s policy system closes large gaps in task correctness, enforcing structured workflows, safe intent handling, reliable tool usage, and controlled output formatting across all model families (Claude Opus – 4.5, GPT OSS 120B and GPT – 4.1) with accuracy improvements ranging from 15% to 26%. Authority is enforced through least-privilege disclosure, explicit compliance rules, and human escalation paths. Intelligent actions are proposed, while authority is exercised by policy and oversight mechanisms. Reasoning is autonomous; decision rights are constrained. CUGA is also a key component in the IBM Think Sovereign Core launch.

Recent findings suggest that case Study 2: Condition-based Maintenance of Physical Assets for IBM Global Real Estate - directed acyclic graph. [14],[15].

Industry observers note that enterprise maintenance systems collect copious amounts of asset data but are unable to effectively combine them, demanding experts to manually piece together fragmented signals and make decisions without unified, evidence-based insights. Our recently launched Maximo Condition Insights [16] agent analyzes large-scale asset data across thousands of assets and locations (sensors, work orders, failure modes and events analysis), using structured evidence and validation loops to reliably identify concerns, prioritize actions and support decision-making with consistent, traceable insights. We have piloted this agent (using GPT OSS 120B) internally with IBM Global Real Estate (GRE), reducing asset analysis time from 15-20 mins to 15-30 sec (a 97% improvement) and increasing asset review coverage from ~1% to ~30% spanning over 120 sites and 6K physical assets. Using AssetOpsBench, the Condition Insights agent reduced unsupported claims by 57%, cut verbosity by 35%, improved rule compliance by 30%, maintained near-zero contradictions, and lowered token usage by on average 77%, while slightly increasing diagnostic specificity. This agent, equipped with a directed acyclic graph, provides structural engineering and operational context to reduce unsupported reasoning under naive prompting, while constraint-aware prompting markedly improves rule adherence, reduces verbosity, and lowers overall token consumption without introducing instability.

In a recent development, summary and References: We have benefited from guides for centuries, which have simplified and enhanced our lives. As technology has evolved, so have the guides we use, enabling us to do more and further shrink our global village. With the arrival of this agentic AI era, as we seek to further enhance society in part through economies of scale, we should continue this trend and fully leverage agent logic to simplify model context and intelligently traverse enterprise workflows at the core; only then will scalable adoption at optimal operating costs be truly feasible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that today we’re releasing Mellum2, an open Mixture-of-Experts model optimized for low-latency text-and-code workloads.
  • Industry observers note that in our technical report, we evaluate Mellum2 across code generation, reasoning, science, and math benchmarks.
  • The MoE architecture keeps total model capacity high while activating only a subset of parameters for each token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today we’re releasing Mellum2, an open Mixture-of-Experts model optimized for low-latency text-and-code workloads. Mellum originally started as a code completion model. With Mellum2, we extend that foundation to a broader set of natural language and software engineering tasks while keeping the model focused on efficient inference and deployability. Modern AI systems increasingly rely on multiple model calls: routing, retrieval, summarization, planning, validation, and tool use. Many of these operations are latency-sensitive and do not require the largest available model. Mellum2 targets these workloads.

Industry observers note that in our technical report, we evaluate Mellum2 across code generation, reasoning, science, and math benchmarks. Mellum2 is competitive with similarly sized open models while delivering more than 2x faster inference, making it suitable for high-throughput production workloads. Model architecture Mellum2 is a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

The MoE architecture keeps total model capacity high while activating only a subset of parameters for each token. This makes inference more efficient and helps reduce serving cost for real-time workloads. Mellum2 is intentionally focused on text and code rather than multimodal tasks. This specialization keeps the model compact and efficient for software engineering workloads.

Mellum2 works well as a lightweight routing and orchestration model in multi-model systems, including prompt classification, tool selection, and intermediate control-flow steps.

The model is well suited for latency-sensitive retrieval pipelines, including context compression, summarization, and retrieval post-processing.

Mellum2 can be used for agent subtasks such as planning, validation, transformation, and context preparation, reducing the need to invoke larger models for intermediate operations.

Because Mellum2 is open and efficient to serve, it can be deployed in self-hosted environments involving proprietary code or internal data.

Industry observers note that as AI systems mature, the most effective architectures are becoming less monolithic. A single frontier model can be powerful, but production systems often need several specialized components working together: retrievers, routers, code-aware models, validators, tool callers, and larger reasoning models. We think of Mellum2 as a “focal” model: a fast, well-scoped model optimized for high-frequency tasks inside larger AI systems. The goal is not to replace every model in the stack. The goal is to make the stack faster, cheaper, and easier to control.

If you are building AI systems for software engineering – inside an IDE, in a RAG pipeline, as part of an agent workflow, or on private infrastructure – Mellum2 is ready to try.

Newark Museum of Art restores ownership of David Drake jug to artists’ descendants

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in Newly introduced Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in Newly introduced Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852. Just a few months later—lightning speed in museum time—The Art Newspaper has learned that the institution has reached an agreement with Drake’s heirs to restore ownership of the work and purchase it back for its permanent collection.

Sources indicate that the arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back. Momentum built from there and return agreements were reached with institutions including the Telfair Museums in Savannah and the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, and others.

Sources indicate that “What happened this July was really special,” indicates George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family. A letter the Newark Museum sent to the artist’s descendants and shared with The Art Newspaper states: “We acquired a jug by your ancestor in 2022 to help us more powerfully teach the history of enslavement and enslaved labour, as part of the 2023 reimagining and reinstallation of our American art galleries, Seeing America: 18th and 19th Century.” Noting the MFA Boston partnership, the museum extended the opportunity to meet and “identify ways we might collaborate”.

According to Lisa Funderburke, the Newark Museum’s director and chief executive, it was the museum’s senior director of registration and collections management, Amber Germano, who first approached her over the summer and asked if she would be willing to sign a letter.

“It’s not uncommon for curators to visit my office with a stack of papers of things that are either for consideration or ongoing engagement on articles of repatriation,” Funderburke notes. “Always my first question is: ‘Can you articulate to me what we’re doing here and what the impulse behind that is?’”.

According to Yaba Baker, one of Drake’s fourth great-grandsons, Funderburke credited her staff with the initial action. “Lisa understood immediately what needed to be done,” Baker indicates. “One thing my family all agreed on: Dave is such a powerful figure in art history and Black history that to take the pots out of public view would be a disservice.”.

Recent findings suggest that things moved quickly after that, with additional family meetings and Funderburke’s conversations with board members and other leaders at the museum. “I felt like this would be a strong north star for our board about where we are and where we want to be, and position ourselves as a museum into the future,” the director claims.

Sources indicate that after the museum commissioned several appraisals of the ceramic vessel, a value of around $135,000 was decided on. Numerous Drake pots have sold for five- and six-figure prices; the current record at auction for one of his works is the $1.65m paid for his 25-Gallon Poem Jar (1858), achieved at Crocker Farm Auctions in Maryland in 2021.

“Our approach is this should not be a zero-sum game,” Fatheree claims, describing the outcome in Newark as a “win-win”.

Sources indicate that baker concurs, stressing the enduring lessons of Drake’s legacy. “He was a slave. He was considered three fifths of a person by the US constitution,” Baker says, adding that anti-literacy laws in South Carolina at the time forbade teaching enslaved people to write.

“For our family, it’s telling the story of someone who was considered by a lot of people to be nothing, but he conducted himself with such excellence,” Baker says, before quoting a famous inscription Drake wrote on another of his vessels that begins, “I wonder where is all my relation”, and concludes: “Friendship to all.”.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1463 w)

CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the organization was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
  • A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.
  • The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the organization was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.

A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.

The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.

“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the organization had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”.

But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the firm’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].

The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.

The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

Recent findings suggest that the following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.

Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”.

A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.

The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”.

“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

In a recent development, ihme stated RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the tech giant could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.

Sources indicate that A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.

But Ihme said a review of the manufacturer’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.

It has been revealed that A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.

“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”.

Industry observers note that indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.

It has been revealed that the Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.

In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.

According to recent reports, “The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”.

The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.

“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”.

According to recent reports, ihme mentioned RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the manufacturer’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.

“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme remarked. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”.

The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is presently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.

Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

Industry observers note that in July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

  • The 2019 SI definition fixes Avogadro's constant exactly:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Counting molecules by weighing them is a two-step conversion with a scale problem attached. The chemistry is straightforward — mass divided by molar mass gives moles, and moles times Avogadro's constant gives particles. The engineering difficulty is numerical: particle counts overflow intuition, floating point has fixed relative precision, and a molar mass assembled from rounded atomic weights shifts the last digits of every result.

The 2019 SI definition fixes Avogadro's constant exactly:.

Two conversions connect the scales:.

It has been revealed that molar mass is a sum of standard atomic weights from the periodic table. For NaCl: 22.98976928 (Na) + 35.45 (Cl) = 58.43976928 g/mol. Those weights are interval quantities in reality; the conventional values are what calculators use, so two tools can differ in the third decimal of the molar mass and disagree in the final particle count.

The guard is worth keeping: a zero molar mass produces Infinity, and a negative mass silently produces a negative particle count.

As a precision reference, 18.015 g of water with M = 2(1.008) + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol is exactly 1.000 mol by construction, or 6.02214076e23 molecules to the precision shown. The round trip is exact in floating point because 5.0 / M * M returns 5.0 here, but that is not a guarantee for arbitrary inputs.

According to recent reports, for a conversion that handles the magnitude and formatting for you, see the Avogadro calculator. The Avogadro guide explains molar mass, formula units, and where the rounding actually enters.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last March, we released Holo3, our state-of-the-art computer-use model.
  • In a recent development, people want to run the same computer-use capabilities across desktop and mobile environments, with seamless integration with different agent frameworks.
  • This is why we are releasing the Holo3.1 family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last March, we released Holo3, our state-of-the-art computer-use model. Adoption was immediate. Developers, enterprises, and partners started deploying Holo3 across a wide range of workflows, from browser automation and business software to internal tools and desktop applications. As adoption grew, we realized performance alone was no longer enough.

In a recent development, people want to run the same computer-use capabilities across desktop and mobile environments, with seamless integration with different agent frameworks. They want deployment flexibility, from cloud inference to fully local execution on end-user devices.

This is why we are releasing the Holo3.1 family. Holo3.1 improves robustness across the three dimensions that matter most in production: environments (web, desktop, mobile), agent frameworks, and deployment targets. For the first time, we release quantized checkpoints optimized for local inference, including FP8, Q4 GGUF, and NVFP4.

Holo3.1 is a major step toward our vision of universal computer-use agents: systems that can operate across environments, integrate into any agent stack, and run wherever the workflow lives.

Based on the Qwen family, Holo3.1 was designed to improve robustness across the environments where computer-use agents are actually deployed, while retaining state-of-the-art performance.

As teams moved Holo3 from evaluation to production, we repeatedly observed the same challenge: strong performance in one setting does not necessarily transfer to another. Mobile devices, alternative agent harnesses, and different execution frameworks all introduce their own sources of distribution shift.

In a recent development, holo3.1 expands Holo3's capabilities beyond browser and desktop control, delivering major gains on mobile environments. On AndroidWorld, our 35B-A3B model improves from 67% to 79.3%, while the smaller 4B and 9B variants improve from 58% to 72%.

To better support teams deploying Holo inside third-party agent stacks, Holo3.1 introduces native support for function-calling protocols in addition to the structured JSON outputs already available in Holo3.

Industry observers note that across OSWorld and our internal benchmark suite covering e-commerce, business software, and collaboration workflows, function-calling and native execution now achieve near-parity performance. Holo3.1 also delivers more than a 25% improvement over Holo3 when evaluated inside our Holotab product harness.

To further enable local and on-device inference, we are also releasing newly introduced model sizes including small models (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) for cost-effective and private deployment, in addition to the larger 35B-A3B model for state-of-the-art performance.

Recent findings suggest that performance versus cost for the Holo3.1 and Qwen 3.5 families. Overall performance averages the four H Corporate benchmarks first (so each family is equally weighted), then takes the mean across OSWorld, AndroidWorld, H Corporate, ScreenSpot-Pro, and OSWorld-G.

This is our first release to ship quantized weights. We’re starting with 35B-A3B checkpoints, available in FP8, Q4 GGUF, and NVFP4.

In a recent development, for NVFP4, we used NVIDIA's Model Optimizer in a W4A16 configuration. These checkpoints enable fast local inference for Computer Use Agents with little to no degradation in model performance. FP8 and NVFP4 achieve the same OSWorld scores, only about two points below the full-precision BF16 checkpoint.

The speedups are substantial: on DGX Spark, NVFP4 W4A16 delivers 1.41× the total token throughput of FP8 and 1.74× that of BF16.

We also release Q4 GGUF checkpoints aimed at local deployment of Computer Use Agents on consumer hardware.

The agent itself runs locally on a Windows or Mac machine, while the model can either run on that same machine—we include reference numbers for Apple Silicon—or on a DGX Spark on the same network. In both cases, execution stays fully private and local, with nothing leaving the user's network.

On Spark, agent harness optimizations we developed with NVIDIA combined with the NVFP4 quantization above deliver a compound ~2× end-to-end speedup over the FP8 baseline, cutting average step time from 6.8s to 3.3s.

Agent request rate across platforms and precisions. On DGX Spark, vLLM with NVFP4 achieves the highest request rate in both Default and Fast modes, followed by Q4 GGUF and FP8. These improvements and more will land in an upcoming desktop agent harness.

The Holo3.1 family is available in four sizes:.

We are also releasing optimized FP8, NVFP4, and Q4 GGUF checkpoints for local and edge deployment.

We look forward to seeing what developers build with Holo3.1.

Three Agents, One Repo: The Coordination Problem Nobody Designed For

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, one coding agent is a productivity tool.
  • In a recent development, the infrastructure conversation covers fleet orchestration and control planes.
  • The mechanical collision is the friendly one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one coding agent is a productivity tool. Two agents in the same repository is a sociology experiment. Three is a coordination problem that most teams solve for the first time in production, on a Friday.

In a recent development, the infrastructure conversation covers fleet orchestration and control planes. It skips the boring, decisive question: what happens when two agents touch the same file at the same time, and who resolves what they did to each other?

The mechanical collision is the friendly one. Two agents edit the same lines, git refuses to merge, and the failure is loud. Everyone notices. This is the good case, because the system mentioned no.

It has been revealed that the semantic collision is the dangerous one. Agent A changes the meaning of a function's return value. Agent B, working from the old contract, builds a feature that reads it. The merge is clean. The tests each wrote still pass in isolation. The system now believes two incompatible things, and nothing failed anywhere.

The duplicate collision is the expensive one. Two agents, given overlapping tickets, build the same feature twice with different names. Both PRs look competent. One of them is pure waste, and until someone notices, both are load.

It has been revealed that none of these are exotic. They are the exact failure modes human teams have, at a speed that breaks the human mechanisms we built to catch them.

Human teams coordinate through standups, hallway conversations, and ownership maps. "I'm touching the auth module, don't start there." It is informal, inefficient, and it works.

Agents attend no standup. They hold no grudges, share no memory, and read no hallway. The coordination layer has to become explicit, which means it has to become infrastructure:.

In a recent development, A claim queue. Work is assigned or claimed, and a claim is visible. No two agents start the same ticket because the ticket remarked who started it. This is a work queue, not a scheduler, and it can be a spreadsheet before it is a platform.

An ownership map. Which files, modules, and decisions belong to which stream of work. Agents respect boundaries they are told about. They cannot respect boundaries nobody wrote down.

In a recent development, A merge gate between agents. Agent PRs that touch adjacent areas wait for the earlier one to land. Serializing the hot paths costs throughput and buys correctness, which is a trade humans already make every day.

A human integration owner. When agent PRs collide, a person who owns the integration decides. Not because humans are faster. Because someone has to be accountable for the seam, and accountability does not delegate to a process.

Industry observers note that 💡 Pro-tip: the semantic collision is the one to design against first. The mechanical one confirms itself. The semantic one ships clean, passes its own tests, and gets discovered by a customer. A shared contract check between agents working in the same area is worth more than any lock.

In a recent development, two or three agents on one repo is not a fleet, and the interesting failures will not always reproduce on demand. Solo developers with a single agent can skip all of this. The problem arrives the first time someone parallelizes "funnel all the open tickets to the agents" without anyone asking which tickets share a codepath.

There is also a real risk of over-engineering: most teams need a claim queue and a merge order, not a control plane, on day one.

In a recent development, but the direction of travel is obvious. The team now includes non-human contributors, and every org-design problem humans ever had, multiplied by speed and stripped of social instinct, is coming to a repository near you.

It has been revealed that how many agents touch your repo before the first collision, and who resolved it? Was it loud, or was it clean?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After the reject, the workers keep looping.
  • I ran his version on the same shape.
  • According to recent reports, the reject lands at the same moment in both arms, 275 to 277 milliseconds across the four runs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After the reject, the workers keep looping. That is the hole in yesterday's pre-fill piece, and sunnatulla_dev found it before I did. In his run, tasks 6 to 9 started at 301 to 421 milliseconds, after the call had already rejected at 272, and a second later every slot read ok. So the array calls them skipped, they ran, and anyone who retries them runs them twice. His fix is one line: set stopped = true in the catch, and let the workers check while (!stopped && ...) before picking up the next task.

I ran his version on the same shape. Ten tasks, three workers, task 4 throwing after 150 milliseconds. Same delays as yesterday, both arms twice, and both repeats came back identical. The flag works. It also leaves two tasks double-running, and those two are the interesting part.

Here is the shape, with the flag in:.

According to recent reports, the reject lands at the same moment in both arms, 275 to 277 milliseconds across the four runs. The flag costs nothing on wall time, because it does not stop anything that is already running. It only stops latest pickups, and there is nothing to pick up until a worker finishes a task.

Industry observers note that read the no-flag row first, because it is worse than it sounds. At the reject, seven slots read skipped. A second later, none of them do. Tasks 5 to 9 started after the call had already failed and finished fine, and tasks 2 and 3 were still running when the reject landed and finished fine too. The array drifts under the caller. A retry built from the reject-time snapshot runs all seven again. Seven tasks doing real work twice, because the label was written before the work happened and nobody updated it after.

In a recent development, the flag arm fixes five of the seven. Tasks 5 to 9 never start. A second later they still read skipped, and this time the label is true: nothing ran there, nothing will, and a retry runs each of them exactly once. That is the whole win, and it is a real one. Five phantom runs gone, for one line and zero measurable cost.

Sources indicate that but look at the last row. Two double-runs survive the flag, and they are tasks 2 and 3, the pair that was mid-flight when task 4 threw. The flag cannot reach them. They are inside an await when stopped flips to true, and the loop condition is only checked after the await resolves. They finish, they write ok into their slots, and the caller that read "skipped" at reject time retries them anyway. In my run they finished 24 and 44 milliseconds after the reject. The window is small. The double-run is not.

According to recent reports, this is the part the one-line fix cannot close. The flag answers the question "has a worker picked this up yet" at the moment of the reject, and for the two in-flight tasks the honest answer at that moment is "yes, and it is not done". The array states skipped because nothing has written anything else yet. There are only two ways to tell the truth about those two slots. One is to mark a task "running" when the worker picks it up, so the caller can see the difference between untouched and in-flight and decide what a retry means for each. The other is to wait before retrying: let the stragglers land, read the array again, and retry only what still reads skipped after everything has settled. The first costs a line. The second costs a delay, and the delay is the honest price of a retry you can trust.

In a recent development, so sunnatulla_dev is right, and the flag is worth adding, and it is not the whole fix. Add it. It turns seven double-runs into two, for free. Then mark the in-flight tasks, or wait for them, because the two that survive are the ones doing real work when the batch falls over, and they are the ones a blind retry will run twice. A stopped flag stops the queue. It stops nothing that already started.
