#80399. Latest Update: How to Stay Informed But Not Overwhelmed by Election News

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1713 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How to Stay Informed But Not Overwhelmed by Election News

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you pick up your phone to check one thing—perhaps the weather, a text message, or the score of a game.
  • Election season can make the news feel unusually personal.
  • There is even a name for this experience: election stress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you pick up your phone to check one thing—perhaps the weather, a text message, or the score of a game. A few minutes later, you have read three election headlines, watched a clip from a debate, skimmed dozens of comments, and somehow learned that democracy, the economy, your health care, and the future of the planet may all be in danger before breakfast.

If this sounds familiar, you are not alone.

Election season can make the news feel unusually personal. The complications on the ballot can affect our finances, health, schools, communities, and rights. At the same time, the way we now encounter political information—constantly, emotionally, and often in fragments—can leave us feeling overloaded rather than informed.

There is even a name for this experience: election stress. The Mayo Clinic describes it as the overwhelming anxiety some people feel during an election cycle. And surveys from the American Psychological Association suggest that elections have become a significant source of stress for many Americans. In the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, for example, 72% of adults said they were worried that the results could lead to violence, and 56% said they feared the election could mark the end of democracy in the United States.

It has been revealed that it is understandable to feel unsettled when an election seems to carry serious consequences. But anxiety is not always a problem to get rid of; in small doses, it can direct our attention toward what matters. It may motivate us to learn, vote, volunteer, have difficult conversations, or support people affected by political decisions.

The problem begins when information meant to help us engage instead keeps our nervous systems in a constant state of alarm.

Part of election stress comes from the uncertainty it elicits. We do not know who will win, what policies will change, or how the people around us will respond. Research suggests that uncertainty itself can be stressful because people naturally want to understand and predict the environment around them. When we feel unable to do that, we may feel less safe and less in control.

In a recent development, news can intensify that uncertainty. Negative news is often more attention-grabbing than positive news, and conflict, danger, and outrage make especially compelling headlines. That does not mean journalists are intentionally trying to harm us. Reporting on threats and problems is an essential part of journalism. But a steady diet of alarming information can shape how we feel about the world, especially when it leaves little room for context, solutions, or signs of human cooperation.

This can create a difficult cycle. When people feel anxious, they often seek out more information in an effort to regain a sense of control. Yet the more election news they encounter—particularly news marked by uncertainty, conflict, and emotional intensity—the more anxious they may feel. Then they check again.

In other words, we may turn to the news to calm ourselves down, only to leave feeling more activated than before.

According to recent reports, political stress is not new. But the way we receive political information has changed dramatically.

When John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon debated on television in 1960, viewers watched in a far more contained media environment. There was no endless stream of clips, reactions, memes, push notifications, and commentary arriving at every hour of the day. People could discuss the debate afterward, but they were not also carrying the debate around in their pockets.

According to recent reports, today, election news can follow us almost everywhere: to the grocery store line, the waiting room, the car, the dinner table, and bed. Social media makes it easier for people to participate politically and amplify voices that were once excluded from public conversation. Those are meaningful benefits. But the same technology can make political information feel impossible to put down.

It also encourages us to consume news in small, emotionally potent pieces. A headline while brushing our teeth. A video clip while waiting for coffee. A dramatic post at a stoplight. These snippets can provoke strong feelings without giving us enough context to understand the story fully.

Sources indicate that that matters because headlines often tell us what to feel before they tell us what happened. Pew research found that five out of eight Americans (63%) remarked they only read news headlines rather than full news articles, specifically when scrolling through social media. When people repeatedly take in emotionally charged fragments of news, they may feel a growing sense of threat while having less detailed information to guide their judgments.

Faced with this constant emotional demand, some people keep checking the news compulsively. Others decide they have had enough and stop paying attention altogether.

News avoidance can offer temporary relief. If every upgrade makes you tense, angry, or helpless, closing the app may feel like self-protection. In fact, a report from the American Press Institute found that a third of Americans want to disengage from news because it feels stressful and overwhelming.

Tips for managing election stress while building a better democracy.

But avoiding news altogether comes with costs, especially during an election year. It can make it harder to participate in democratic life, understand complications that affect our communities, or distinguish reliable reporting from misinformation passed along by friends, influencers, or highly partisan accounts.

The goal, then, is not to consume more news or no news. It is to develop a healthier relationship with news: one that helps us stay informed without asking our nervous systems to be on call all day.

According to recent reports, 1. Choose a news source that includes solutions, not only problems. During stressful times, it can help to seek out reporting that does more than identify what is going wrong. Constructive journalism still covers serious problems, but it also provides context, examines solutions, and asks what people and communities can do next. This approach is not about pretending everything is fine. It is about giving readers a more complete picture: What is the problem? Who is affected? What is being tried? What can citizens realistically do? Solution-oriented reporting may be especially helpful during elections because it can replace helplessness with a more grounded sense of agency and hope for the future.

Recent findings suggest that when you choose a news source, consider asking: Does this reporting leave me better informed? Does it help me understand the problem, or does it only make me feel alarmed? Does it explain possible solutions as well as the threat?

2. Balance distressing news with inspiring media. We do not need to force ourselves to be positive about difficult realities. But we can balance the emotional weight of election coverage with media that remind us of human goodness, beauty, courage, and connection.

Research suggests that stories of kindness, moral courage, and collective care can evoke feelings such as elevation, gratitude, and hope. These emotions can broaden our view of what is possible and help us feel more connected to other people. And upcoming research from the University of Santa Barbara suggests that these emotions can even reduce stress.

This might mean watching a short video about neighbors helping one another after a disaster, reading a profile of local organizers working across differences, listening to music that helps you settle, or returning to a film or show that leaves you feeling more hopeful about people, or nostalgic about the past.

Industry observers note that think of this as building a more balanced media diet. Election news can be an important part of that diet, but it should not be the only thing we feed our minds. Just as eating one healthy meal a week does not transform our physical health, one inspiring story will not undo chronic stress. Over time, though, regularly choosing media that restore us, physically and mentally, can help cultivate resilience, hope, and perspective.

3. Create boundaries around when you check the news. Finally, consider treating news less like a snack and more like a meal.

Recent findings suggest that snacking on news all day can mean consuming a lot without ever feeling nourished. You absorb a headline here, an alert there, and a few comments in between—but never get enough context to make sense of what you are seeing. The result can be a lot of emotional calories and very little understanding.

Instead, choose one or two intentional times to engage with the news. You might read a full article over breakfast, listen to a trusted news program on your commute, or set aside 15 minutes at lunch to review the day’s major stories. If you are prone to checking headlines compulsively, digital wellness strategies such as app limits or notification settings can make those boundaries easier to keep.

According to recent reports, it may also help to avoid making late-night news “snacking” part of your bedtime routine. By the end of the day, our emotional and cognitive resources are often already depleted. A stream of alarming headlines can quickly turn into doomscrolling: the repeated consumption of negative online content that leaves us more agitated and less able to sleep.

Giving news its own place in the day does not mean becoming indifferent. It means making room to take in information carefully, in context, and with enough emotional space to respond thoughtfully.

Election stress is real because elections matter. Feeling concerned about the future does not mean that something is wrong with you; it may mean you are paying attention.

Sources indicate that but paying attention does not require constant exposure to distress. We can choose reporting that informs and empowers us, balance difficult coverage with media that reminds us of human possibility, and set boundaries that give our minds a chance to rest.

According to recent reports, the aim is not emotional numbness. It is becoming the kind of informed citizen who can face difficult news, stay connected to what matters, and still have enough calm and hope left to act.

It has been revealed that sophie H. Janicke, Ph.D., is a positive media psychologist working as an associate professor at Chapman University, who investigates the role that latest and traditional media play in promoting and affecting character development, self-transcendent emotions (such as elevation, gratitude, and awe), prosocial behavior, and happiness.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pallant House Gallery in Chichester, southern England, does not own any paintings by the self-taught Cornish artist Alfred Wallis (1855-1942). But it does own many works by the early 20th-century artists who were heavily influenced by the former fisherman and rag-and-bone merchant, who first took up painting with pots of house paint and sheets of cardboard as a lonely widower aged 70.

Sources indicate that alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist gathers together works by Wallis and by artists who visited, lived in or worked in St Ives, including Barbara Hepworth, Peter Lanyon, Margaret Mellis, Adrian Stokes, John Wells, Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, Ben and Winifred Nicholson and Christopher Wood. It was Ben Nicholson and Wood who first befriended Wallis in 1928 when they peered in astonishment into his tiny dark cottage stuffed with paintings.

Many of the Wallis paintings—of tilted houses and harbours, ships and stormy seas, under lowering grey skies—originally acquired as gifts or bought for a few shillings, are now being borrowed from private collections and museums including the Tate, Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge and Aberdeen Art Gallery. A private collector is loaning a unique collaborative work: a half-finished view of a Brittany quayside by Christopher Wood, which Wood gave to Wallis who then completed it.

In a recent development, A record price of £184,000 was set at a Christie’s auction last year for a work by Wallis, who once remarked to a buyer: “gimme what you like for ’em”. Ben Nicholson, barely earning himself and with a young family, bought his first Wallis painting for half a crown; Wallis once sent a bundle of paintings to the collector and curator Jim Ede for ten shillings. When the artist died in 1942, a roll of uncashed postal orders was found on his mantelpiece. He was only saved from a pauper’s grave by the St Ives artists.

Winifred Nicholson’s Seascape with Two Boats (1932) Photo: © Kettle’s Yard, University of Cambridge; © Trustees of Winifred Nicholson.

The exhibition is curated by James Scott, an orthopaedic surgeon, who first discovered Wallis when, as a bored medical student, he spent days in Sotheby’s auction rooms, watching sales and afterwards tracing the buyers out of curiosity.

Recent findings suggest that scott insists there was neither condescension nor exploitation in the relationship between Wallis and Nicholson and the other art school educated artists. Hepworth wrote that Wallis never knew “how much we all learnt from him”.

The St Ives artists “discovered him when they were looking for a latest direction, experimenting with a restricted palette and flattened picture plane,” Scott says, “and they found he was already doing it and doing it better.” Wallis learned nothing from them, continuing his own unmistakable style until weeks before his death.

According to recent reports, scott treasures two works by Wallis. “I’ve often thought maybe the time has come to sell them, and then I come downstairs and see them on the wall and think no, I can’t, I love them more and more.”.

• Alfred Wallis: an Artists’ Artist, Pallant House Gallery, Chichester, 21 November-2 May 2027; Penlee House, Penzance, 15 May 2027-9 October 2027.

  • The Purple, one of the upcoming card faces, fills its surface with a dotted halftone field in deep violet, and the name sits small in a light grotesque at the top left, next to the chip.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wolff Olins builds the Hyundai Card brand identity on Architect of Change: a fixed core, and a generative color system for every card.

The card is the poster here. The Purple, one of the upcoming card faces, fills its surface with a dotted halftone field in deep violet, and the name sits small in a light grotesque at the top left, next to the chip. The same violet bleeds into a painted field behind the card, so object and world share one color. Wolff Olins spent time in Seoul before drawing anything, talking with customers and young Koreans. More than eight in ten South Koreans in their twenties still live with their parents, so people define themselves through taste and through what they choose to carry. A card indicates something about who you are and who you intend to become, and that became the design problem.

The system runs on a simple split. A fixed core never moves: the logo sits in the same place, in the same open bracket frame, carried by the same typeface on every card. Around that core, each card gets its own world. The entry cards, M, X and Z, use a generative system of bright color and repetition, so no two faces repeat the same pattern. A type specimen sheet sets the grotesque in full, and the card specification drawing marks the 1.58 ratio every face must hold.

Recent findings suggest that scale does the talking in the applications. The wordmark stays small and bracketed while a single figure, 93 percent, fills a whole green panel, and the card faces run at poster size on street walls. The card ratio repeats across posters, totes and packaging, so the system reads as one object cut to different sizes.

It has been revealed that the physical pieces carry the same discipline. Modular packaging holds the whole range together: a grey box with a debossed Hyundai Card mark and a red peel tab, each card sealed in a protective layer that peels back to reveal its character. The dotted halftone on the Purple card reads as texture before it reads as pattern. The tote bag carries the bracketed wordmark on green, with a black band at the base.

Color is the flex in the system. Violet owns the Purple card, acid green owns the commercial card and the big figures, and black and grey hold everything together. The butterfly image indicates what the generative color does when it leaves the card: the same violet, painted loose across a wing, with the pattern breaking into dots. Every card keeps the same bones and gets a different skin.

#80394. What’s Crucial to Us When Making Political Decisions?

What’s Crucial to Us When Making Political Decisions?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1491 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy issues.
  • In a recent development, the paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans.
  • “When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” stated Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy issues. But a latest study by UC Berkeley social scientists finds that Americans usually don’t consider the full scope of difficult issues, instead basing their opinions on mental shortcuts that sidestep complexity.

In a recent development, the paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans. While some people in the study did closely analyze a range of issues before coming to an opinion, others did a quick back-of-the-napkin tally of plusses and minuses, or even more commonly based their opinions on just one factor, the authors found.

“When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” stated Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak. But, he added, “we find that most of them aren’t. Most commonly, people rely on a mental shortcut, effectively deciding based on the single factor they care about most and largely ignoring the rest.”.

According to recent reports, for example, when asked to choose between two fictional U.S. Senate candidates based on age, gender, race, education, military experience, and political experience, many of the study participants would make their decision based on just one of those factors.

According to recent reports, that doesn’t mean that people are irrational, said coauthor Nidhi Banavar, a Berkeley cognitive scientist. “The kind of rationality that we define in the paper is quite different from what many humans actually do in real life,” she explained. “We have these amazing brains, but they’re not the infinite computational machines that would be necessary in order to do the kind of ‘rational’ we imagine in our paper.”.

Still, the findings have clear implications for politics and political communication. For example, Banavar remarked, if a leader knows that public opinion on climate change is dominated by pocketbook concerns to the exclusion of other complications, then that single factor might weigh heavily in political advertising. Complex science issues, meanwhile, might be downplayed.

The paper, “Classifying Strategy Use in Multi-Attribute Subjective Choice: Application to Conjoint Experiments in Political Science,” was published recently in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Bansak is an associate professor of political science at UC Berkeley; Banavar is a postdoctoral researcher in political science at UC Berkeley.

The foundational ideals of American democracy grew from the Enlightenment era some three centuries ago. Central to that framework was a belief that humans, being rational, are capable of governing themselves—and justified in demanding political power. A core concept has been the marketplace of ideas, a constant competition between political and policy goals, looks, and analysis that would inform citizens and help them to govern themselves.

While many eras in U.S. history feature episodes in which reason faltered, modern social scientists have detailed the ways in which cognitive bias, rational ignorance, and other behaviors short-circuit reasoning. Still, the hopeful assumption about human reasoning persists.

Social scientists have long studied human decision making at the aggregate level. Banavar and Bansak set out to build a new kind of cognitive model, a complex tool that can enable researchers to see an individual’s decision making mid-process, in detail.

The model doesn’t give them a view into the minds of their research subjects, but the researchers can study hundreds or thousands of decisions by an individual; from these patterns, they can perceive the values and reasoning processes that shape their decisions.

In all, nearly 3,800 people were involved in the study. Each participant sat at a computer screen, and the computer generated a random set of choices in three areas: which migrants they would rather admit to the United States, which Senate primary candidate they would rather vote for, and which climate policy package they would prefer the United States to adopt.

In a recent development, consider the basic question comparing two hypothetical migrants to the U.S. Their profiles appeared side by side, each described by six factors: region of origin, education level, gender, age, English proficiency, and whether they were seeking economic opportunity or asylum. The research subject would have to choose which of the migrants they preferred to admit to the U.S.

According to recent reports, the computer randomly presented 30 different sets of hypothetical migrants. If a participant consistently chose the younger migrant or the migrant with greater English skills, for example, the researchers could conclude that that was the most key factor for that participant.

In a recent development, the same decision framework was presented for comparing potential climate change policies and fictional U.S. Senate candidates.

The research did yield some insights about basic priorities: Participants preferred younger political candidates. They preferred climate change policy that minimized economic impact on their household. They preferred immigrants who were seeking asylum as opposed to seeking economic opportunity, and those who were below retirement age.

According to recent reports, but that wasn’t the primary purpose of the study. Banavar and Bansak were less interested in what participants decided, and more interested in how they decided.

The results were striking: In 68% of the cases, study participants used shortcuts and did not deeply assess all six factors when choosing between hypothetical Senate candidates, migrants, or climate policies.

In a recent development, nearly 54% indicated a pattern of making choices dominated by one of the six factors. Another 14% took a different shortcut: Given six factors for each candidate or policy, they counted the total number of factors that they preferred for each, then chose the one containing the greater number.

Industry observers note that how many used a comprehensive evaluation of all six factors—a rational assessment, without any shortcuts? Just under 30%.

Interestingly, Banavar noted, a majority of participants did not consistently stay with the same strategy. Some might rely on just one factor in choosing a climate policy, while more fully weighing all the factors in deciding which migrant to admit.

Sources indicate that “You can’t put people into buckets to say, ‘OK, this is someone who’s actually only going to care about only one thing,’” she noted. “People are actually relating differently to each of these different domains and choosing to use different levels of effort, for want of a better term.”.

To understand why people shift strategies will require further research, she said.

In a recent development, the study comes with some important caveats: If a participant favored female candidates, for example, or migrants who were seeking political asylum, and if both choices had those attributes, the participants had to consider other factors. That reduced, but did not eliminate, the pattern of making a choice based on one factor.

But when the researchers asked the participants to rate each profile before choosing one of them, the participants were more inclined to consider all factors in making their choices.

Further, the researchers allowed for only two attributes in their comparisons—male or female, for example, white or Black, or aged in their 50s or 70s. That’s not ideal, Banavar said, but to include multiple races, for example, is too complex for the cognitive model, and would dilute the patterns in the data. In the choice of Senate candidates, the study did not include the fictional candidates’ political parties. That question could provoke such strong, reflexive reactions that it would cloud the findings, she said.

In a recent development, the authors say their research has notable implications not just for cognitive research, but for real-world, on-the-ground U.S. political processes.

Often, Bansak mentioned, our understanding of public opinion is based on surveys that ask people to choose between complex options defined by many factors. The upcoming research shows analysts that individuals often base their opinions on a single factor, and that can create a clearer picture of what people want in public policy, and why they want it.

“This bears directly on how we interpret the kind of public-opinion and preference data that routinely informs policy debates and news coverage,” he remarked.

And that understanding, Banavar stated, can shape the policy process—and political communication. If leaders present issues in layers of complexity, “how much are people going to read or listen to that?” she asked. “What is the thing that’s really notable to them, given a particular issue? That’s completely lost when you don’t think about the decision-making process.”.

Can You Learn to Feel More Loved?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you.
  • In our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love.
  • Industry observers note that in our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you. Or a friend who is just there to listen without telling you what you should have done differently. We don’t tend to think of these experiences as grand declarations of love, but they leave us with a certain lingering warmth: the feeling of being loved.

In our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love. This emphasis shifts attention away from the expressions of love (i.e., loving signals). While expressions are actions we choose to take, felt love is an internal, subjective sensation that washes over us. However, how strongly it does so also depends on us: The same act of care may pass unnoticed or land as love, based on the receiver’s cognitive beliefs or state of mind. Many experiences may elicit felt love, and they occur not only in romantic settings, but when we share time with friends, receive supportive gestures from family, or even get unexpected help from strangers. We are only just beginning to uncover how people come to feel loved and whether that experience can be changed—if it can be learned, like a skill.

Industry observers note that in our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S. population to judge situations that would make most people feel loved. What they ranked most love-eliciting was being shown compassion in difficult times—an act that, in principle, any person could (and should) offer. Pets feeling happy to see them ranked highly for eliciting the feeling of being loved. Clearly, love, as people live it day to day, reaches past courtship and partnership.

It has been revealed that work like this partly drives how we measure who feels loved and when. It is common for studies to measure the experience of love as if it were a stable trait—for example, romantic attachment as a demographic indicator—but this practice obscures fundamental aspects of the lived human story. Relationship status may describe part of someone’s circumstances, but it does not tell us whether that person feels loved in their daily experience. For example, many people experience love while unattached, and many do not experience love despite being in a long-term relationship. In fact, in our studies, strong experiences of felt love are reported by participants who identify as unattached. To study felt love, we also have to ask about the experience directly.

According to recent reports, subjective states like felt love are inherently volatile, so studying it requires many careful observations, ideally while people are going about their daily lives. We often rely on complex research methods that focus not only on how people feel at a given time, but on the patterns of change over time and how those are shaped by our environment and affected by others. Our basic approach is simple in principle: Ask people how loved they feel at different times while they go about their lives. In two studies published in 2020, in which over 200 participants reported their felt love states a handful of times per day for several weeks, we found that people with higher levels of felt love also tended to report greater flourishing and emotional well-being.

It has been revealed that frequent, repeated observations also allow us to disentangle a person’s typical experience from day-to-day fluctuations. This can also reveal individual differences in how persistent daily felt love states are—a feeling can be strong and brief, or weaker but sustained. Persistence is not automatically desirable: A below-usual feeling of being loved can persist, too. Whether particular patterns directly affect well-being remains an important open question.

In a recent development, to study the role of persistence, we developed custom mathematical models that include love inertia—that is, how long that warm feeling stays with us. In our recently published study, 52 participants reported how loved they felt as well as how much love they had expressed over a period of 28 days. We found that people whose felt love states were more persistent also enjoyed better mental health and indicators of well-being. Even more interestingly, the more people expressed love to others in their daily lives, the more they themselves tended to feel loved in return. Expressing love appears to be a gift that keeps on giving: Showing love is associated with a lasting sense of warmth and better well-being, and it also spreads love around you.

Industry observers note that this finding suggests an actionable insight: Expressing love could be one route to feeling loved. If you are feeling a lack of connection, proactively expressing selfless care for someone else might help jumpstart your own feelings of being loved. We don’t yet know what accounts for this association. Expressing love might invite a warm response, change how you interpret a relationship, or be part of an interaction that lifts both people up.

Can an interaction actually change how loved someone feels? A 2024 study with 218 parent–child pairs argues just that. The authors of that study randomly assigned parents and their children, aged eight to 13, to one of two nine-minute conversations. In one condition, they took turns answering questions that encouraged personal disclosure (for example, instead of a surface-level question like “How was school?,” they might ask, “What is something you worry about?”). In the other condition, they made small talk. Children in the disclosure condition reported feeling more loved during the conversation.

This result cannot readily be explained by children in warmer families simply choosing more personal conversations—assignment of children to conditions was random. The researchers changed the conversation and observed a direct difference in the children’s experience.

Such findings need to be independently replicated for reliability and generalizability, but this is an important and promising step: A straightforward intervention changed an experience of feeling loved. The next question we can work on is whether changes of this kind can become part of daily life.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Sources indicate that our focus on the receiver side of love brings a slightly more complex perspective: that an act does not produce a loving feeling by itself, but that effect is moderated by interpretation and expectation—thoughts that come to us in the moment, cognitive beliefs that support those thoughts, and the justifications we have for those beliefs. A colleague’s quiet help can be experienced as love, or dismissed as routine professional courtesy.

An area that is not yet well-explored is how the reception of expressions of love can be taught. If feelings follow perceptions, and perceptions follow beliefs, then felt love is a cognitive phenomenon in addition to an emotional one, so that cognitive skills contribute to how we experience the social world. It may be possible for people to learn to notice when they reflexively dismiss acts of care, to check their interpretation against what actually happened, and to re-evaluate in order to let the sender’s kindness count. It is also possible that a deficit in this cognitive skill prohibits many people from benefiting from the ambient love that is already present in everyday life. Even so, biased perceptions can have positive effects in this context. People with a stronger general tendency to interpret daily life experiences as expressions of love feel more loved in general, with all the well-being benefits that brings.

We now have ways to measure felt love in daily life, evidence linking it to well-being, and at least one experiment that changed it in the moment. A sensible next step is to connect those findings.

Recent findings suggest that can an intervention change daily feelings of love for weeks or months? Does that change lead to better well-being? Does it work for people who start out feeling relatively unloved, or mainly for those already doing well? Those are different questions, all embedded in the vastly complex network of our daily environments and experiences—part of what is sometimes called the exposome—and they require different, carefully drawn comparisons.

According to recent reports, future trials could focus on the cognitive component of felt love—whether an underlying ability to appreciate acts of love extends to other facets of life, and whether interventions should target the individual’s reasoning before focusing on their social context. Repeated measurements in daily-life settings could be used to show whether any differences generated by the intervention survive after the study session. Such trials would need to be designed with a great deal of care to establish the mechanisms of causality—a standard challenge of daily-life social psychology studies, but an especially critical one here. Establishing how to make experiences of felt love more available is an expansive but worthwhile scientific endeavor.

Sources indicate that finally, an emerging focus on love also recognizes how it is culturally and contextually bound. While certain loving gestures are found all over the world (such as helping someone in need, or empathic attention), to foster intercultural understanding, empathy, and inclusivity in diverse societies, it is vital to recognize love’s cultural variations in everyday life. We are at the moment conducting global cross-cultural research to identify specific ways love is shown in everyday life across different types of relationships, beyond just the romantic.

Recent findings suggest that while we and other researchers continue to conduct larger studies to unpack these exact mechanisms, we don’t have to wait for the data to start paying closer attention to the quiet moments in our own lives. What happens when you feel genuinely cared for? What happens when you proactively express love to someone else? Being mindful of how they respond can reveal something that checking a box to count affectionate gestures misses. Fostering these experiences doesn’t require a laboratory—it is a daily practice we can all begin right now. Showing love is a low-cost experiment we can all conduct in our own daily lives.

People with vitamin B12 deficiency were three times more likely to be suffering this problem.

People with vitamin B12 deficiency were three times more likely to be suffering this problem.

Feeling depressed can be a sign of vitamin B12 deficiency, a study finds.

People with a vitamin B12 deficiency are three times more likely to be experiencing ‘melancholic’ depression.

Melancholic depression mostly involves depressed mood.

Some of the other most common symptoms of depression are decreased interest in life or pleasure, energy loss and concentration problems.

The study also found a link between low folate intake and depression.

Folates include vitamin B9, folacin and folic acid.

People with a low intake of folates were 50 percent more likely to be experiencing melancholic depression.

The research included 2,806 Finnish people whose nutritional status and depression symptoms were assessed.

Although vitamin B12 and folates were linked to melancholic depression, the same link was not seen with non-melancholic depression.

Symptoms of non-melancholic depression cluster around anxiety and low self-esteem, with less emphasis on depressed mood.

Dr Jussi Seppälä, the study’s first author, said:.

“The findings have practical implications in the care of patients with depressive symptoms.

For example, it may be wise to avoid medication causing weight gain among patients with non-melancholic depression, whereas melancholic depressive symptoms may call for a closer look at the quality of the patient’s diet.”.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is easy to rectify with supplements or by dietary changes.

The body uses vitamin B12 to make red blood cells and to keep the nervous system healthy.

Other common signs of vitamin B12 deficiency include experiencing muscle weakness and being constipated.

Meanwhile, some of the best dietary sources of folates include:.

Folate levels are particularly high in chickpeas, yeast extract, lentils and broad beans.

The study was published in the Journal of Affective Disorders (Seppälä et al., 2012).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Could correcting this vitamin deficiency make a difference for people already receiving treatment for depression?
  • Vitamin D supplements may ease symptoms in some people with depression, according to a review of the evidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could correcting this vitamin deficiency make a difference for people already receiving treatment for depression?

Could correcting this vitamin deficiency make a difference for people already receiving treatment for depression?

Vitamin D supplements may ease symptoms in some people with depression, according to a review of the evidence.

Several small trials found improvements, including in people who started out with low vitamin D levels.

Other trials found little or no benefit, and one large study found that supplements did not lower the chances of developing depression.

The link is plausible because vitamin D may influence inflammation and chemical signalling in the brain, both of which are relevant to mood.

Depression itself could also lower vitamin D levels if it leaves people with less energy to go outdoors.

That makes it important to ask two separate questions: whether correcting a deficiency can help someone who is already depressed and whether taking vitamin D can prevent depression in the first place.

Researchers at the University of Oradea reviewed studies measuring vitamin D levels in people with and without depression, as well as trials testing whether supplements changed their symptoms.

One small trial recruited people who had both major depression and a vitamin D deficiency.

Both groups continued with their usual care, but after about three months, depression scores were lower in the group given a vitamin D injection than in the placebo group (Vellekkatt et al., 2020).

Differences in who took part, the doses they received and how symptoms were measured made the trials difficult to compare.

A trial designed to test prevention followed more than 18,000 adults aged 50 and over who had no clinically relevant depressive symptoms when they joined.

Over about five years, participants who took daily vitamin D were about as likely to develop depression or clinically relevant symptoms as those who took a placebo (Okereke et al., 2020).

Vitamin D receptors are found in parts of the brain such as the hippocampus, which is involved in memory and the response to stress.

The vitamin can also influence immune signals involved in inflammation.

This is one route through which it might affect mood in some people with depression.

Vitamin D levels also reflect habits that can change during depression, including what people eat and how much time they spend outdoors.

Someone who stops going for regular walks, for example, may get less sunlight and make less vitamin D as a result.

A blood test taken during an episode of depression cannot tell which change came first.

The question now is whether correcting a vitamin D deficiency can improve symptoms in people already receiving treatment for depression.

Answering it will take larger trials that recruit people with both conditions and follow them long enough to see whether any improvement lasts.

The study was published in the journal Pharmaceuticals (Roșian et al., 2025).

How Young People Are Researching Problems That Matter to Them

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.
  • Middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code.
  • It has been revealed that many youth across the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.

Middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code. They engaged in research to explore how administrators, teachers, and staff could incorporate their voices in decision-making processes. Students conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers and developed recommendations for their school, including more student-led events and a more active role engaged in school policy discussions. The following semester, the principal added students to several school leadership committees, where they helped inform programs and policies beyond the dress code, such as student social events and classroom curricular activities.

It has been revealed that many youth across the U.S. report feeling disengaged and disconnected from their schools, which is associated with declining attendance and greater mental health challenges. Addressing these challenges is critical, especially because a sense of belonging and connectedness predicts attendance, academic success, social well-being, self-esteem, and other positive outcomes for students.

Research is one crucial way to seek out solutions to these problems, and Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) is an innovative and growing approach that engages youth as experts to improve their lives, communities, and youth-serving institutions. In middle and high schools across the U.S., students in YPAR classes conduct research to inform policies, practices, and peer education efforts. They have prioritized and addressed a wide range of academic and school-climate concerns, such as improving teacher-student relationships, peer relationships, safety, and school lunch options; and reducing disproportionate discipline, substance use, and transit barriers.

In schools that provide opportunities for YPAR, students are trained to take up roles as researchers, knowledge producers, and changemakers who contribute to their school communities. Further, YPAR evidence can deepen adults’ understanding of what shapes students’ feelings of belonging, patterns of engagement, and well-being. YPAR findings thus can inform more relevant and responsive solutions that can benefit youth, adults, and the broader community. This article provides guidance for educators who work with K–12 students and are interested in implementing YPAR.

Here are three examples of how YPAR impacts different levels of the school “ecosystem.”.

Systems-level: High school YPAR students in an Ohio school district explored whether their school provided adequate mental health services. They conducted a schoolwide survey, and their findings revealed that although there were mental health services available, many students were not aware of them. In response, the student researchers took action and developed more promotional materials and held informational assemblies to raise awareness of these services. They also held meetings with teachers, counselors, administrators, and the superintendent to discuss potential districtwide solutions to improve mental health services and access.

Relationships: Middle school YPAR students in a California school district identified that they didn’t feel supported by their teachers. To explore this concern further, they conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers on teacher-student relationships. Their findings offered concrete suggestions on how teachers could improve their mentorship relationships with students, including practicing active listening, showing respect and compassion, being more flexible with assignments, and incorporating more engaging classroom activities that lift up student voices. The students also recommended student-led teacher evaluations.

Sources indicate that student-level: High school YPAR students in a California school district conducted English and Spanish focus groups with their peers on attendance and belonging. Based on their findings, the YPAR students proposed buddy programs to connect new students with their peers, schoolwide workshops to raise awareness on racial stereotyping, and lunchtime soccer tournaments to increase a sense of belonging.

Read more stories on our YPAR Hub.

Our YPAR Design Guide offers several considerations when deciding whether YPAR is a fit for your program or setting. YPAR has been primarily implemented with middle and high school students, and is well-suited to strengthening the developmental capacities of youth in early, middle, and late adolescence. However, elementary school students have also engaged in successful YPAR projects using mapping and arts-based methods.

First, adult facilitators (for example, teachers or program leaders) should assess capacity and consider whether there are adequate resources to pursue the YPAR project, including the timeframe of the project, staffing required, whether funding is needed, and the setting and scope.

Second, adult facilitators can introduce YPAR to students in a way that meets them “where they are at.” Not every student will be interested in YPAR from the start. Some may have had limited exposure to research, and others may not have had positive experiences (for example, through a particularly challenging or frustrating class assignment). Facilitators can engage the students in activities that lift up their experiences, then generate excitement by framing research as a tool for exploring and taking action on the challenges that students care about.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Facilitators should also work with students to clarify their motivations for the project: What is the purpose of the project? What do students hope to get out of participating in YPAR? And what does their desired impact look like? In several projects, we have seen students become more interested in YPAR as they move through the process, analyze data, and develop their action aims and recommendations.

Finally, adult facilitators should be attentive to the broader context surrounding the topic or problem. For example, if the research is on safety and well-being, what programs or initiatives are already focusing on these issues, both in and out of school (for example, community health organizations)? What are the relevant constraints (for example, barriers accessing decision-making processes)? And where might there be opportunities to partner and collaborate? Understanding these factors will help adult facilitators and students choose an area of focus that aligns with their goals.

Recent findings suggest that YPAR is not “one size fits all.” Adult YPAR facilitators adapt YPAR across a multitude of settings, including schools, afterschool programs, and community-based organizations such as youth centers. Even within schools, a YPAR process can vary in length. For example, some YPAR projects span a single unit within a semester; others may take up an entire semester, and in some cases extend across a full academic year (fall and spring semesters).

Further, YPAR is sometimes conducted as part of a club or extracurricular activity outside of formal class time. While the structure and duration of YPAR projects vary, many projects follow these steps: building the team, identifying and defining an problem or problem, selecting a research design and methods, collecting data, analyzing and interpreting results, developing action looks and recommendations, disseminating findings, and taking action.

Throughout the YPAR process, young people serve as leaders who decide on the topic, issue, and questions they wish to investigate. Adult facilitators serve as supportive guides and mentors, training them in research methods focused on generating numerical data or text- and image-based data. Youth then go on to collect and analyze their data and develop actions prepares and recommendations to address their selected problem.

A core value in YPAR is authentic power-sharing between adult facilitators and youth researchers. Most of the time, youth navigate learning spaces where they are “receivers” of knowledge from adults. Further, in traditional adult-led research projects, youth typically serve only as “respondents” to surveys or interviews, with no say in the research questions, methods, or interpretation.

You can learn more about YPAR practice and research by accessing the following resources: YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson aims and other resources YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. Locate our YPAR online training modules here. IRB resources for researchers who want to study YPAR and a supplemental article.

YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson looks and other resources.

YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. Locate our YPAR online training modules here.

IRB resources for researchers who want to study YPAR and a supplemental article.

Recent findings suggest that the YPAR approach challenges these dynamics by positioning youth as knowledge generators who combine lived-experience expertise with systematic data-based inquiry. Youth researchers have decision-making power and are primary drivers of the YPAR process, while adults serve as guides to help them in advancing their projects.

In a recent development, power-sharing is a learnable and teachable set of skills. Our guide provides lessons and activities that help facilitators attend to power dynamics, along with strategies that support power-sharing throughout YPAR. Adults and youth can productively share power in research when supportive structures are in place.

The results from YPAR research may (or may not) result in policy or practice change. Adult facilitators play a critical role in strategically connecting YPAR evidence to key decision-making spaces and helping implement youth action aims.

One step that facilitators can take is identifying existing decision-making structures where there may be opportunities to integrate YPAR evidence. They can also determine whether fresh routines need to be established. High School youth in Colorado investigated practices (through student surveys) that they noticed enhanced student-teacher relationships. Students then developed and led a day-long professional development for teachers on how small adjustments to the start of the year, including taking time to build trust and rapport before reviewing the syllabi, could increase student engagement and buy-in.

In our work, students have consistently emphasized how much it matters for adults to “keep them in the loop,” reporting back on whether and how their YPAR evidence was used. Authentically integrating YPAR evidence involves being transparent with students and following up with them throughout the process. Adults should take YPAR evidence seriously and actively prevent tokenizing processes—in other words, where YPAR evidence becomes a check-the-box rather than meaningful engagement. Ultimately, adults supporting YPAR must take an active role in creating conditions where youth feel safe, heard, and valued.

There is growing interest in YPAR at the local, state, and national levels, and it aligns with many initiatives that are already happening in schools. For example, the National Institutes of Health identified YPAR as a promising approach to address conditions that affect mental health and well-being, such as social isolation and exposure to unsafe environments. In California, SB997 mandates student voice be integrated in school and district budgeting processes. Oregon, Ohio, and New Jersey have similar mandates that require youth voice in decision making. There are strong synergies between YPAR and social-emotional learning programs, which are implemented in many school sites. YPAR also aligns with many academic competencies and standards, offering students a unique opportunity to build durable academic and career skills.

Students care about their schools and want to improve them. Adults need to learn along with them, listen to them, value their ideas, and support them in making change.

Four Practices to Help You Feel More Engaged at Work

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, work can be tough.
  • While some difficulty at work may always be expected, there are things we can do to take control of our work lives and bring more kindness, appreciation, connection, and trust into the workplace.
  • Industry observers note that you can find some of these on Greater Good in Action, our library of over 100 practices found to improve well-being.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, work can be tough. With only 20% of workers feeling engaged globally, we need tools that can help boost engagement and well-being at work.

While some difficulty at work may always be expected, there are things we can do to take control of our work lives and bring more kindness, appreciation, connection, and trust into the workplace. For many years, researchers have been testing different practices that individual employees, managers, and teams can do to improve work life for everyone.

Industry observers note that you can find some of these on Greater Good in Action, our library of over 100 practices found to improve well-being. Each practice includes:.

Recently, we added four new practices that you might want to try in your workplace.

Let’s face it: We don’t always feel appreciated at work, even though appreciation seems to be a key need for most people. In this practice, you begin a regular team meeting with the simple act of appreciating the person to your left. You say something specific about one of their qualities or an action they took and the impact it had on you. Then that person appreciates the person to their left, and you go around the room (or virtual meeting) until everyone gets appreciated.

It has been revealed that years ago, I tested this practice in a meeting with a team I was working with. When we got to the third person being appreciated, she broke down into tears. She remarked, “I’ve been working here for nine years, and I didn’t know you guys appreciate me. . . . I didn’t even know you liked me.”.

Help everyone on your team feel appreciated to boost connection and performance.

While this was hard to hear, it’s also a problem that is pretty easy to fix. Appreciation Circles, which can be repeated regularly, try to establish a culture and ritual of appreciation so that no one has to feel undervalued at work.

This practice is designed for managers during their regular (and sometimes less than inspiring) one-on-one meetings with their direct reports. It recommends that you ask employees these three questions:.

According to recent reports, as managers, sometimes we don’t realize the impact of our time with employees. Research suggests that our supportive behaviors can go a long way to helping employees feel more engaged. So how can managers be more supportive?

Improve employee satisfaction and engagement with a guided conversation.

One study found that when managers encouraged, assured, and valued employee efforts, employees felt more engaged. These are the themes that the three questions in this practice address.

In a recent development, the question of how you build trust has always been a fascinating one for me, because trust is so foundational to getting things done and is such an vital part of a healthy workplace culture. Studies suggest that high-trust work cultures are often higher-performing, but how do you actually earn trust at work?

Sources indicate that in their analysis of hundreds of studies on trust, researchers found that there are three key levers for building trust: demonstrating your ability, benevolence, and integrity. In other words, people trust you more when they believe you can get things done, have their best interests at heart, and follow through on your word.

Demonstrate your trustworthiness to your coworkers.

This practice helps you identify ways to show others that you have these qualities by considering three questions and then acting on your answers:.

This practice is probably one of the more fun and feel-good practices because it encourages you to offer some random acts of kindness to your coworkers and see if this creates a multiplier effect in your workplace.

For example, you could bring a coworker a cup of coffee, help them with a project, or offer a handwritten thank-you note.

Do something nice for coworkers and watch kindness spread.

Studies suggest that kind and helpful behaviors can be contagious to those receiving the kind acts, and that even bystanders see boosts in their well-being just from observing these acts.

Sources indicate that we encourage you to try this low-risk and feel-good practice in your workplace soon—as well as the rest of them! Keep in touch and let us know how these practices land in your workplace.

Industry News: Older Brains Lose Synchronization Between Movement and Body Temperature

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken.
  • Industry observers note that throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography.
  • Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken. Simultaneously, aging decouples movement from internal temperature regulation and triggers neuroinflammatory gene shifts, glial remodeling, and neuronal loss inside the brain’s master circadian clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).

Industry observers note that throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography. Governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a tiny cluster of neurons in the hypothalamus that acts as the brain’s master biological clock, core body temperature, hormone release, and physical activity rise and fall in predictable ~24-hour circadian rhythms.

Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.

While age-related sleep fragmentation and impaired temperature regulation are well-documented clinical hallmarks of aging, precisely how ultradian rhythms evolve across the lifespan, and how they relate to cellular changes inside the SCN, has remained poorly understood.

Now, a comprehensive chronobiology investigation examining mice across the adult lifespan (from 3 to 21 months of age) reveals that while the 24-hour circadian framework remains detectable in old age, the faster 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms deteriorate, accompanied by a breakdown in coordination between physical activity and internal body temperature.

To separate externally driven daily routines from internally generated biological timing, the researchers continuously recorded locomotor activity and core body temperature in mice across multiple age brackets under both standard 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycles and constant darkness, an experimental condition that removes environmental light cues to expose the brain’s intrinsic pacemaker.

The physiological telemetry revealed a striking divergence between macro- and micro-rhythms:.

To explore the neural underpinnings of these physiological shifts, the investigators analyzed cellular architecture and gene expression profiles directly inside the SCN of young and aged mice.

Even though core circadian clock genes continued cycling, the cellular microenvironment of the aging SCN showed pronounced signs of biological wear:.

By demonstrating that shorter ultradian rhythms and temperature-activity coupling falter even when overall 24-hour circadian rhythmicity persists, the findings offer a fresh lens through which to view age-related sleep disturbances and vulnerability to heat or cold stress.

Further experimental work will determine whether targeting neuroinflammation or supporting glial-neuronal communication inside the SCN can restore ultradian stability, potentially paving the way for interventions that alleviate sleep fragmentation and thermoregulatory decline in older adults.

What is the difference between circadian rhythms and ultradian rhythms?

In a recent development, circadian rhythms are biological cycles that repeat roughly every 24 hours, such as the daily sleep-wake cycle. Ultradian rhythms are shorter biological cycles that repeat multiple times within a single day, typically every 2 to 6 hours, regulating smaller bursts of physical activity, alertness, and core body temperature fluctuations.

How does aging affect these biological rhythms?

According to recent reports, researchers found that while older mice kept their basic 24-hour rhythms and core clock gene cycles, their shorter 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms weakened significantly. Furthermore, physical movement and internal body temperature became disconnected, no longer rising and falling together as closely as in younger animals.

What changes happen inside the brain’s master clock during aging?

Inside the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the brain’s master clock, aging was linked to increased activity of immune-related genes, changes in supportive glial cells, and a reduction in neuron density, which may impair how the brain coordinates fine-tuned daily bodily rhythms.

Funding: This study was supported by JSPS KAKENHI (grant numbers JP21K19287, JP21H05036, JP23H04941, and JP22K21351); AMED (grant number JP21zf0127005); JST CREST (grant number JPMJCR24T4); JST SPRING (grant number JPMJSP2124) and the World Premier International Research Center Initiative (WPI).

Aging remodels the suprachiasmatic nucleus and weakens ultradian rhythms and activity–temperature coupling.

Aging alters daily physiology, but how these changes relate to remodeling of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) remains incompletely understood.

Here, we examined time-resolved SCN transcriptomic profiles alongside longitudinal recordings of core body temperature and locomotor activity, using separate cohorts for the molecular and physiological analyses.

Aging was associated with extensive SCN transcriptomic remodeling, including enrichment of innate immune, interferon-related, complement-associated, and glial programs, while selected canonical clock genes retained detectable rhythmic expression.

Recent findings suggest that the composition and temporal profiles of broader rhythmic transcriptional programs also differed between young and aged SCN samples. Aged mice retained detectable circadian rhythms but indicated reduced 2–6 h ultradian wavelet power in locomotor activity and body temperature, lower activity–temperature correlations, and altered optimal integration windows and time-of-day-dependent relationships. Histological analyses revealed glial remodeling and reduced neuronal marker-positive cell density in the aged SCN.

These findings identify parallel age-associated changes in SCN molecular and cellular organization and in physiological rhythmic power and activity–temperature associations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers discovered that taste buds actively process and filter mixed flavors before sending signals to the brain. The study indicates that sour stimuli trigger serotonin release inside taste buds, dampening neural responses to sweet, bitter, and salty flavors while downstream neurons sort tastes into two broad categories: pleasant or unpleasant.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Industry observers note that biting into a tart lemon bar or sipping a sweet-and-sour beverage delivers a complex blend of chemical stimuli to the tongue simultaneously. For decades, neuroscientists have worked to determine whether the brain mixes these individual flavor signals centrally, or whether taste buds themselves edit and shape flavor combinations before a single electrical impulse ever leaves the tongue.

Industry observers note that in a study published in Journal of Neuroscience, neuroscientists led by Dr. Stephen Roper at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine recorded gustatory nerve signaling in mice exposed to mixed taste solutions.

The findings reveal that sourness exerts a dominant, suppressive effect over other primary tastes right inside the taste bud, driven by local serotonin signaling.

To trace how mixed tastes travel from peripheral receptors to the central nervous system, Roper and colleagues measured neural responses along the gustatory pathway while exposing mice to single tastes and multi-taste mixtures.

Comparing neural firing across taste conditions revealed two striking principles of gustatory coding:.

To uncover how sourness mutes competing tastes so early in the sensory pipeline, the investigators zeroed in on serotonin, a neurotransmitter released inside each taste bud by specialized sour-responsive receptor cells (Type III taste cells).

Manipulating local serotonin levels directly controlled the strength of flavor suppression:.

These results demonstrate that taste buds function as miniature computational hubs, using paracrine serotonin signaling to inhibit neighboring receptor cells before gustatory information is handed off to cranial nerves.

According to recent reports, “Taste buds not only respond to and transduce taste compounds, they also integrate and manipulate gustatory signals before transmitting them to the brain,” explained Roper. “The neurons that collect signals produced in taste buds are themselves organized into two large groups or clusters, neurons that convey gustatory signals associated with pleasure and neurons that convey unpleasant taste signals.”.

By establishing how peripheral serotonin signaling shapes flavor dominance and how downstream neurons sort palatability, the study lays groundwork for identifying the genetic signatures of pleasure- versus aversion-coding taste neurons, and exploring whether targeted molecular interventions could one day modulate taste perception in clinical nutrition or sensory disorders.

Why do sour flavors overpower sweet, salty, and bitter tastes?

Researchers at the University of Miami found that sour-responsive cells inside taste buds release the neurotransmitter serotonin. This local serotonin dampens the signals of neighboring sweet, bitter, and salty receptor cells before the taste information even reaches the nerves leading to the brain.

Do taste buds simply send raw flavor data to the brain?

In a recent development, no. The study shows that taste buds act like miniature processing centers that actively mix, filter, and modify taste signals locally before transmitting them to sensory neurons.

How do taste nerves organize flavors on their way to the brain?

According to the researchers, the sensory neurons collecting signals from taste buds are broadly organized into two major functional groups: neurons that carry pleasant taste signals and neurons that carry unpleasant taste signals.

Sour Suppresses Sweet, Salty, and Bitter: Implications for Signal Processing in Taste Buds.

Taste is typically encountered as complex blends, yet how peripheral taste organs process heterogeneous mixtures remains poorly understood. Here we asked how sour stimuli influence the encoding of sweet, salty, and bitter tastes in primary gustatory sensory neurons.

According to recent reports, using in vivo calcium imaging in mice of either sex to record neurons in geniculate ganglia during oral delivery of tastants, we compared responses to naturally occurring taste stimuli presented alone versus in binary mixtures that activate acid (sour)-sensing (Type III) taste bud cells. Adding citric acid or HCl robustly suppressed sucrose-evoked responses in geniculate ganglion neurons, even though acid itself did not activate those neurons.

Industry observers note that acid-induced suppression generalized to bitter and salty tastes, which, like sucrose, are believed to activate Type II taste cells. Additional stimuli that activate acid-sensing taste cells (NH4Cl, KCl) also reduced sucrose responses, supporting a common mechanism linked to Type III cells. Manipulating levels of serotonin (a paracrine transmitter released by Type III cells) in taste buds altered taste suppression: increasing serotonin with 5-hydroxytryptophan enhanced acid-induced suppression whereas depleting serotonin with para-chlorophenylalanine weakened it.

Industry observers note that finally, population analyses, including UMAP dimensionality reduction, indicate that taste suppression is not limited to a particular subset of gustatory sensory neurons. The findings are consistent with serotonin-dependent paracrine inhibition within taste buds as a contributor to sour-driven suppression in taste mixtures and reveal a compression of gustatory information into hedonic categories as early as at the level of primary sensory neurons.
